claim: XPD is a 5'-3' translocating SF2 helicase (SF2B)
source: XPD is a prototypical 5′–3′ translocating SF2 helicase (SF2B) (Singleton et al., 2007; Wolski et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Singleton et al., 2007; Wolski et al., 2010)

claim: XPD consists of four structural domains: helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2), ARCH domain, and FeS domain
source: It consists of four structural domains: helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2), which contain all helicase signature motifs important for coupling ATP binding and hydrolysis to directional translocation along ssDNA, and two unique modular domains (ARCH and FeS) inserted in the conserved motor core (Figure 1A; Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies and reference to Figure 1A showing the domain structure

claim: HD1 and HD2 domains contain all helicase signature motifs important for coupling ATP binding and hydrolysis to directional translocation along ssDNA
source: It consists of four structural domains: helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2), which contain all helicase signature motifs important for coupling ATP binding and hydrolysis to directional translocation along ssDNA, and two unique modular domains (ARCH and FeS) inserted in the conserved motor core (Figure 1A; Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies

claim: All known SF2B enzymes participate in DNA repair or support replication
source: All known SF2B enzymes participate in DNA repair or support replication and, therefore, are important for maintenance of genomic integrity (White, 2009; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Human XPD is a player in nucleotide excision repair and transcription initiation
source: Human XPD is a player in nucleotide excision repair and transcription initiation (Egly and Coin, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Related FeS-containing helicases FANCJ, RTEL and CHLR1 share structural organization with XPD
source: Related FeS-containing helicases FANCJ, RTEL and CHLR1 share structural organization and likely the same unwinding mechanism as XPD (Gupta et al., 2007; White and Dillingham, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Related FeS-containing helicases FANCJ, RTEL and CHLR1 likely share the same unwinding mechanism as XPD
source: Related FeS-containing helicases FANCJ, RTEL and CHLR1 share structural organization and likely the same unwinding mechanism as XPD (Gupta et al., 2007; White and Dillingham, 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural similarity and citations to prior literature

claim: Monomeric XPD unwinds duplex DNA in 1-bp steps
source: We show that monomeric XPD unwinds duplex DNA in 1-bp steps, yet exhibits frequent backsteps and undergoes conformational transitions manifested in 5-bp backward and forward steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including PWD analysis and step-fitting algorithms

claim: XPD exhibits frequent backsteps during unwinding
source: We show that monomeric XPD unwinds duplex DNA in 1-bp steps, yet exhibits frequent backsteps and undergoes conformational transitions manifested in 5-bp backward and forward steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing backstepping behavior

claim: XPD undergoes conformational transitions manifested in 5-bp backward and forward steps
source: We show that monomeric XPD unwinds duplex DNA in 1-bp steps, yet exhibits frequent backsteps and undergoes conformational transitions manifested in 5-bp backward and forward steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing 5-bp steps and inferred to represent conformational transitions

claim: Forward, single-base pair stepping of XPD utilizes the spontaneous opening of the duplex
source: Quantifying the sequence dependence of XPD stepping dynamics with near base pair resolution, we provide the strongest and most direct evidence thus far that forward, single-base pair stepping of a helicase utilizes the spontaneous opening of the duplex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing sequence dependence of stepping kinetics correlated with duplex opening probability

claim: The proposed unwinding mechanism may be a universal feature of DNA helicases that move along DNA phosphodiester backbones
source: The proposed unwinding mechanism may be a universal feature of DNA helicases that move along DNA phosphodiester backbones.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from XPD findings to other helicases

claim: SF1 and SF2 helicases contain a conserved motor core comprised of a nucleotide binding site in the cleft between two RecA-like domains
source: The two largest helicase superfamilies, SF1 and SF2, contain a conserved motor core comprised of a nucleotide binding site in the cleft between two RecA-like domains (Singleton et al., 2007; Fairman-Williams et al., 2010; Beyer et al., 2013; Raney et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: SF1 PcrA and UvrD helicases translocate along single-stranded NA by 1 nucleotide during each ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle
source: Ensemble kinetic and structural studies of SF1 PcrA (Subramanya et al., 1996; Soultanas et al., 1999; Dillingham et al., 2000, 2002), UvrD (Ail et al., 1999; Fischer et al., 2004; Lee and Yang, 2006) and SF2 nonstructural protein 3 (NS3) (Tai et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1998; Pang et al., 2002; Levin et al., 2004; Tackett et al., 2005; Mackintosh et al., 2006; Gu and Rice, 2010) suggest these domains move as a ratchet-like inchworm, whereby the helicase translocates along single-stranded NA by 1 nucleotide (nt) during each ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior ensemble kinetic and structural studies

claim: SF2 NS3 helicase translocates along single-stranded NA by 1 nucleotide during each ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle
source: Ensemble kinetic and structural studies of SF1 PcrA (Subramanya et al., 1996; Soultanas et al., 1999; Dillingham et al., 2000, 2002), UvrD (Ail et al., 1999; Fischer et al., 2004; Lee and Yang, 2006) and SF2 nonstructural protein 3 (NS3) (Tai et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1998; Pang et al., 2002; Levin et al., 2004; Tackett et al., 2005; Mackintosh et al., 2006; Gu and Rice, 2010) suggest these domains move as a ratchet-like inchworm, whereby the helicase translocates along single-stranded NA by 1 nucleotide (nt) during each ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior ensemble kinetic and structural studies

claim: RecBC and NS3 helicases exhibit unwinding in steps nested within larger steps
source: Ensemble and single-molecule kinetic studies of RecBC (Bianco and Kowalczykowski, 2000; Lucius et al., 2004) and NS3 (Dumont et al., 2006; Myong et al., 2007) have reported unwinding in steps nested within larger steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior single-molecule studies

claim: NS3 helicase unwinds DNA with a single-base pair step size
source: A more recent single-molecule study of NS3 helicase confirmed a single-base pair unwinding step size but also reported 1/2-bp steps, which were attributed to asynchronous release of the unwound NA (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior single-molecule study

claim: NS3 helicase exhibits 1/2-bp steps attributed to asynchronous release of the unwound NA
source: A more recent single-molecule study of NS3 helicase confirmed a single-base pair unwinding step size but also reported 1/2-bp steps, which were attributed to asynchronous release of the unwound NA (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior single-molecule study

claim: SF1B and all SF2 helicases interact with the phosphodiester backbone
source: In contrast to 3′–5′ SF1A helicases, which must remain in register with DNA because its bases are intercalated between aromatic residues of the active site (Velankar et al., 1999; Lee and Yang, 2006), SF1B and all SF2 helicases and related dsDNA translocases interact with the phosphodiester backbone (Singleton et al., 2007; Fairman-Williams et al., 2010; Beyer et al., 2013; Raney et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: 3'-5' SF1A helicases must remain in register with DNA because its bases are intercalated between aromatic residues of the active site
source: In contrast to 3′–5′ SF1A helicases, which must remain in register with DNA because its bases are intercalated between aromatic residues of the active site (Velankar et al., 1999; Lee and Yang, 2006), SF1B and all SF2 helicases and related dsDNA translocases interact with the phosphodiester backbone (Singleton et al., 2007; Fairman-Williams et al., 2010; Beyer et al., 2013; Raney et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

source: This approach allowed us to monitor individual XPD molecules acting on a dsDNA hairpin with base pair resolution.

source: In contrast to other helicases, backstepping plays a prominent role in XPD helicase mechanism.

source: XPD exhibited frequent single-base pair backsteps, which depended on ATP concentration and DNA sequence, and larger backstepping events that likely corresponded to conformational rearrangements of the protein–DNA complex.

source: XPD exhibited frequent single-base pair backsteps, which depended on ATP concentration and DNA sequence, and larger backstepping events that likely corresponded to conformational rearrangements of the protein–DNA complex.

claim: Larger backstepping events in XPD likely correspond to conformational rearrangements of the protein-DNA complex

claim: XPD unwinding relies strongly on spontaneous opening of the base pairs ahead
source: We show that XPD unwinding relies strongly on spontaneous opening of the base pairs ahead, and that this alone accounts for the observed low processivity.

claim: Spontaneous opening of base pairs ahead accounts for the observed low processivity of XPD

claim: XPD exhibited repetitive unwinding bursts during which the hairpin gradually unfolded, then suddenly and completely re-annealed
source: Several features are notable. First, the protein exhibited repetitive unwinding 'bursts' during which the hairpin gradually unfolded, then suddenly and completely re-annealed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Re-annealing during XPD unwinding occurred in large backward jumps of -6.3 ± 1.6 bp (mean ± SD; N = 144 bursts)
source: While unwinding was gradual, re-annealing occurred in large (−6.3 ± 1.6 bp, mean ± SD; N = 144 bursts) and sudden backward jumps (Figure 1D, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements

claim: The re-annealing rate during XPD unwinding was high (>100 bp/s; N = 144 bursts)
source: The re-annealing rate was high (>100 bp/s; N = 144 bursts), much faster than the translocation speed of 13 ± 2 nt/s (Honda et al., 2009) and ATP independent, inconsistent with helicase translocation on the opposite strand, as observed in other systems (Dessinges et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements

claim: XPD translocation speed on ssDNA is 13 ± 2 nt/s
source: The re-annealing rate was high (>100 bp/s; N = 144 bursts), much faster than the translocation speed of 13 ± 2 nt/s (Honda et al., 2009) and ATP independent, inconsistent with helicase translocation on the opposite strand, as observed in other systems (Dessinges et al., 2004).

claim: The ARCH domain of XPD can encircle the translocating DNA strand during unwinding

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies

claim: The ARCH domain encircling the translocating DNA strand provides a potential structural basis for backsliding without dissociation
source: Structures and biochemical studies suggest that the ARCH domain of XPD can encircle the translocating DNA strand during unwinding (Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008; Kuper and Kisker, 2012; Kuper et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012), providing a potential structural basis for backsliding without dissociation (see 'Discussion').

claim: On average, XPD unwound only 12 ± 3 bp (mean ± SD) during each burst
source: After several unwinding bursts and backslides (Table 1), activity suddenly ceased, indicating protein dissociation. In none of our measurements (N = 363 traces) did activity return once a dissociation event was observed. The second notable feature is the low processivity of XPD helicase (Figure 1D). Although the full hairpin measured 89 bp, on average only 12 ± 3 bp (mean ± SD; Table 1) were unwound during each burst.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements summarized in Table 1

claim: No unwinding activity was detected on constructs containing a ssDNA binding site smaller than the expected XPD footprint (0-dT and 3-dT)
source: No unwinding activity was detected on the constructs containing a ssDNA binding site smaller than the expected XPD footprint (0-dT and 3-dT; Figure 2A,B), indicating that XPD helicase could not initiate unwinding of these substrates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: XPD helicase could not initiate unwinding on substrates with binding sites smaller than its footprint
source: No unwinding activity was detected on the constructs containing a ssDNA binding site smaller than the expected XPD footprint (0-dT and 3-dT; Figure 2A,B), indicating that XPD helicase could not initiate unwinding of these substrates.

claim: Unwinding activity was readily detected when the binding sites were ≥10 nt

claim: Two types of unwinding behaviors were observed for long binding sites: low-processivity activity and processive activity
source: Interestingly, we observed two types of unwinding behaviors for long binding sites: a 'low-processivity' activity (Figures 1D and 2C), in which ∼12 bp were unwound repetitively; and a 'processive' activity (Figure 2D), in which the 89-bp hairpin was completely unwound.

claim: The translocating strand passes from the canonical binding site through the opening formed by the ARCH and FeS domains
source: Biochemical and structural analyses (Kuper and Kisker, 2012; Kuper et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012) indicate that the translocating strand passes from the canonical binding site through the opening formed by the two auxiliary domains (ARCH and FeS) and is guided by the residues of HD1 and FeS domains, forming a secondary DNA binding site to the wedge structure on the back of the FeS domain that splits the duplex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical analyses

claim: The secondary DNA binding site accommodates ∼5 nt
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, this site accommodates ∼5 nt.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The observed 5-bp backsteps occur when the translocating strand dissociates from the secondary binding site
source: We propose that the observed 5-bp backsteps occur when the translocating strand dissociates from this secondary binding site, allowing the 5 nt normally occluded to re-anneal with the complementary strand.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on structural data and experimental observations

claim: Dissociation from the secondary binding site renders the helicase incompetent for unwinding until the point of duplex separation reengages the wedge structure
source: This renders the helicase incompetent for unwinding until the point of duplex separation reengages the wedge structure, necessitating reopening of the 5 bp (Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the proposed mechanism and citation to prior work

claim: The observed force dependence of 5-bp backsteps may indicate that higher substrate tensions prevent the displaced strand from binding to the secondary site
source: The observed force dependence of these events (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) may indicate that higher substrate tensions prevent the displaced strand from binding to the secondary site, stabilizing the translocating strand's interaction with this site.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed force dependence

claim: The secondary binding site separates the motor core from the wedge structure that splits the duplex
source: The 5-bp back and forward steps illustrate the importance of the secondary binding site in controlling XPD helicase activity: it separates the motor core from the wedge structure that splits the duplex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural data and the proposed mechanism

claim: Unwinding occurs only when the translocating strand resides within the secondary DNA binding site
source: Unwinding occurs only when the translocating strand resides within this secondary DNA binding site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the proposed mechanism

claim: The secondary binding site allows control of 5'-3' translocation and force generation by XPD
source: This not only allows control of 5′–3′ translocation and force generation by XPD (Kuper et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012), but also stalls the helicase at bulky UV-induced damage, thereby triggering nucleotide excision repair (Mathieu et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The secondary binding site stalls the helicase at bulky UV-induced damage, thereby triggering nucleotide excision repair
source: This not only allows control of 5′–3′ translocation and force generation by XPD (Kuper et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012), but also stalls the helicase at bulky UV-induced damage, thereby triggering nucleotide excision repair (Mathieu et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Confronted with stable sequences (when popen is small), XPD exhibits a higher frequency of backsteps
source: The backstepping behavior of XPD is highly sequence-dependent (Figures 5 and 6). Confronted with stable sequences (i.e., when popen is small), the helicase exhibits a higher frequency of backsteps (Figure 6A).

claim: The linear dependence of kF on popen at saturating ATP suggests a 'passive' unwinding mechanism
source: The linear dependence of kF on popen at saturating ATP suggests a 'passive' unwinding mechanism in which the helicase captures spontaneously opened base pairs at the ssDNA/dsDNA junction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed linear dependence

claim: A strictly passive model requires that the rate be strictly proportional to popen
source: However, a strictly passive model (Betterton and Jülicher, 2005; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2002; Johnson et al., 2007; Manosas et al., 2010) requires that the rate be strictly proportional to popen, whereas the observed linear trend exhibits an offset.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical models from prior literature

claim: The offset in the linear trend of kF vs popen is indicative of an intrinsic destabilization of the duplex by the helicase
source: However, a strictly passive model (Betterton and Jülicher, 2005; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2002; Johnson et al., 2007; Manosas et al., 2010) requires that the rate be strictly proportional to popen, whereas the observed linear trend exhibits an offset. This feature is indicative of an intrinsic destabilization of the duplex by the helicase, characteristic of an 'active' mechanism (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is inferred from the deviation from a strictly passive model

claim: XPD exhibits 'partially' active unwinding where the fork is destabilized by 1.9 kBT through interaction with the protein
source: A global fit to the minimal kinetic scheme incorporating sequence dependence (solid lines, Figure 6A–I) suggests 'partially' active unwinding (Figure 7B). The fork is destabilized by 1.9 kBT through interaction with the protein, yet still slows the XPD's progress.

claim: The fit yields a translocation rate ktrans ≈ 10 nt/s (obtained in the limit that popen = 1)
source: We highlight the fact that the fit yields a translocation rate ktrans ≈ 10 nt/s (obtained in the limit that popen = 1), in excellent agreement with that determined from independent measurements of XPD translocation on ssDNA (Honda et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by fitting experimental data and comparison to prior measurements
